extracted.intended_audience: university educators, philosophers, theologians, and students concerned with the philosophy of knowledge and curriculum
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative standards about the nature of knowledge, the interrelation of sciences, and the proper definition and place of Theology within a university curriculum. Argues for including Theology as a distinct, systematic science and warns against curricular omissions and reductionism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth is the object of Knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth means facts and their relations, which stand towards each other pretty much as subjects and predicates in logic. Knowledge is the apprehension of these facts, whether in themselves, or in their mutual positions and bearings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All that exists, as contemplated by the human mind, forms one large system of facts which resolves into an indefinite number of particular facts with countless relations. Knowledge aims to apprehend these facts and relations; truth is therefore the arrangement and recognition of facts and their bearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sciences are partial abstractions (relations over things)
rubrics_metrics.description: These various partial views or abstractions, by means of which the mind looks out upon its object, are called sciences, and embrace respectively larger or smaller portions of the field of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sciences tell us what things are principally by telling their relations or assigning predicates to subjects. They arrange and classify facts, reduce phenomena under common laws, and trace effects to causes. They do not present whole substantive things as the senses do; each is incomplete in respect to the thing itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sciences need each other; omission prejudices completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The systematic omission of any one science from the catalogue prejudices the accuracy and completeness of our knowledge altogether, and in proportion to its importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because sciences are partial and interdependent, one science often corrects or completes another. A curriculum or intellectual system that excludes a science will have defective apprehension of the whole; examples and consequences are drawn throughout the text (e.g., physics without chemistry or psychology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sciences differ in importance and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: They differ in importance; and according to their importance will be their influence, not only on the mass of knowledge to which they all converge and contribute, but on each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessing sciences requires attention to the breadth of their field and depth of penetration; omission or weakness in a more important science produces greater deficiencies in overall knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy as the integrative 'science of sciences'
rubrics_metrics.description: The comprehension of the bearings of one science on another, and the use of each to each, and the location and limitation and adjustment and due appreciation of them all, one with another, this belongs to a sort of science distinct from all of them, which I call Philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy should coordinate and judge the relations among sciences, showing how each supplements and corrects others; this integrative role is proper to university-level reflection and teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theology is a legitimate science (Science of God)
rubrics_metrics.description: By Theology I mean the Science of God, or the truths we know about God put into system; just as we have a science of the stars, and call it astronomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a God exists, Theology bears on all truth and must be included among the sciences because Divine agency underlies and influences the facts and relations studied by other sciences. Theology's truths, when real, contribute correction and completion to physical, historical, moral, and metaphysical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: What Theology is not (exclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theology is not: (1) Physical Theology (pious/polemical remarks upon the physical world), (2) mere polemics such as 'Evidences of Religion' (supplemental but not identical to Theology), (3) vague 'Christianity' or popular religion incapable of proposition, (4) mere acquaintance with the Scriptures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify the subject-matter: avoid conflating Theology with apologetics, popular religion, or devotional/historical reading of Scripture. Theology should be treated as a systematic intellectual discipline with propositions and doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theology's core doctrinal content (attributes and agency of God)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theology teaches that there is an invisible, intelligent Being (God) distinct from the world, self-dependent, eternal, omnipotent, omniscient, omnipresent, perfectly good, wise, and the Creator and Governor of all things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theological study should systematize doctrines about God's nature (eternity, aseity, perfection), His providential action in creation and history, moral law implanted in rational beings, and the relation of divine agency to the intelligible and moral orders. These items specify what belongs to the science of Theology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include anthropology and moral/mental sciences in the curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: To shut up the subject of anthropology altogether (the moral and mental sciences) would be to omit necessary elements of Education; domestic feelings and manners are not a sufficient substitute for systematic Teaching of the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluding psychology, moral philosophy, or anthropology leads to narrow and unreliable knowledge; university curricula must provide formal instruction in these fields rather than leaving them solely to private or familial instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reductionism: do not explain human or divine agency solely by physical causes
rubrics_metrics.description: A Professor who confines himself to physical causes and denies volition or divine agency is making his particular craft usurp and occupy the universe and is betraying a want of philosophical depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When questions are matters of fact (e.g., whether volition operates in the world), they cannot properly be settled solely by abstract physical theory. Curriculum and teaching should not reduce all phenomena to one class of causes; account for moral and spiritual agents where relevant. The text includes examples (denial of capillary attraction, chemical affinities, influence of mind on bodily health, and the barometer example) to show errors from overreduction.
